Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- A large ice shelf is "imminently" close to breaking away from part of the Antarctic Peninsula, scientists said Friday. Scientists are investigating whether the ice breakup is caused by global climate change. Satellite images released by the European Space Agency on Friday show new cracks in the Wilkins Ice Shelf where it connects to Charcot Island, a piece of land considered part of the peninsula. The cracks are quickly expanding, the ESA said. Scientists are investigating the causes for the breakups and whether it is linked to global climate change. The Wilkins Ice Shelf -- a large mass of floating ice -- would still be connected to Latady Island, which is also part of the peninsula, and Alexander Island, which is not, said professor David Vaughan, a glaciologist at the British Antarctic Survey. The ice shelf experienced a great amount of changes last year, the ESA said. In February 2008, the shelf dropped 164 square miles (425 square kilometers) of ice. In May it lost a 62-square-mile chunk. That meant the "bridge" of ice connecting Wilkins to the islands was just 984 yards wide at its narrowest location, the ESA said. Further rifts developed in October and November, said Angelika Humbert of the Institute of Geophysics at Germany's Muenster University. "During the last year the ice shelf has lost about 1800 square kilometers (694 square miles), or about 14 percent of its size," Humbert said. Antarctica's ice sheet was formed over thousands of years by accumulated and compacted snow. Along the coast, the ice gradually floats on the sea, forming massive ledges known as ice shelves, the ESA says. Several of these ice shelves, including seven in the past 20 years, have retreated and disintegrated. The Wilkins Ice Shelf had been stable for most of the past century before it began retreating in the 1990s. "It had been there almost unchanged since the first expeditions which mapped it back in the 1930s, so it had a very long period of real stability, and it's only in the last decade that it's started to retreat," Vaughan said. Wilkins is the size of the state of Connecticut, or about half the area of Scotland. It is the largest ice shelf on the Antarctic Peninsula yet to be threatened. If the ice shelf breaks away from the peninsula, it will not cause a rise in sea level because it is already floating, scientists say. Some plants and animals may have to adapt to the collapse. The Antarctic Peninsula is the piece of the continent that stretches toward South America.

**Wilkins Ice Shelf close to breaking away from Antarctica, satellite images show**

*By Staff Writer*

A vast slab of floating ice on the Antarctic Peninsula is close to breaking away, scientists say, after satellite images showed new fractures spreading across the Wilkins Ice Shelf and a narrow ice bridge holding the shelf in place rapidly weakening.

The Wilkins Ice Shelf, located on the western side of the Antarctic Peninsula, has been closely watched for years as rising regional temperatures have contributed to repeated breakups. Researchers say the latest satellite evidence suggests the shelf is nearing a major collapse or separation from nearby islands.

Images captured by European and U.S. satellites show long cracks cutting through the ice shelf and the disintegration of an ice bridge that connected the shelf to Charcot Island and Latady Island. That bridge had acted like a pin, helping stabilize the larger shelf. As it fractures, scientists warn the remaining ice could become increasingly vulnerable to breaking apart.

“This ice shelf has been hanging on by a thread,” said one polar scientist familiar with the satellite observations. “Once the bridge is gone, the forces holding the shelf in place are greatly reduced.”

Researchers with the British Antarctic Survey and other polar monitoring groups have described the Wilkins shelf as one of several Antarctic Peninsula ice shelves to show dramatic retreat in recent decades. The region has warmed faster than many other parts of the planet, contributing to surface melting and structural weakening of ice shelves.

The Wilkins Ice Shelf has already suffered major breakups. Large sections collapsed in 1998, and another significant disintegration occurred in 2008, when satellites recorded thousands of square kilometers of ice fracturing and drifting away. Scientists said those events were part of a broader pattern of ice-shelf retreat along the Antarctic Peninsula, including the well-known collapses of the Larsen A Ice Shelf in 1995 and Larsen B in 2002.

Satellite data have been crucial in tracking the changes because the Wilkins Ice Shelf lies in a remote part of Antarctica where direct human observation is difficult. Radar satellites, which can see through clouds and darkness, have allowed scientists to monitor cracks, ice motion and breakup events even during the Antarctic winter.

“The satellite record gives us a clear view of how quickly these systems can change,” said another glaciologist. “An ice shelf can look relatively stable for years, and then a critical fracture can trigger a much larger breakup.”

Despite the dramatic images, scientists say the breakup of the Wilkins Ice Shelf would not directly raise global sea levels because the shelf is already floating on the ocean, much like ice cubes in a glass of water. When floating ice melts or breaks apart, it does not add significant new volume to the sea.

However, researchers caution that ice-shelf collapse can still matter for sea level in other cases. Ice shelves often act as buttresses, slowing the flow of glaciers behind them. If an ice shelf that holds back large land-based glaciers collapses, those glaciers can accelerate into the ocean, contributing to sea-level rise.

In the case of Wilkins, scientists say the immediate sea-level impact would likely be minimal because the shelf does not restrain major inland glaciers in the same way some other Antarctic shelves do. But they say its breakup would be another warning sign of rapid environmental change on the Antarctic Peninsula.

“The Wilkins collapse would not flood coastlines by itself,” a scientist said. “But it is part of a larger story: warming is changing Antarctica’s ice, and some of those changes can have global consequences.”

Climate researchers say continued monitoring is essential as Antarctica’s ice shelves respond to warming air and ocean conditions. While the fate of Wilkins may be regional, they say the processes being observed there are relevant across the continent — particularly in areas where ice shelves help hold back much larger masses of land ice.

**BREAKING NEWS: Wilkins Ice Shelf on Brink of Major Collapse as Antarctic Ice Bridge Fails**

**ANTARCTIC PENINSULA —** A vast Antarctic ice shelf roughly the size of a small U.S. state is on the verge of dramatic collapse after the failure of a narrow ice bridge that had helped hold it in place, scientists monitoring the region said.

The **Wilkins Ice Shelf**, a floating platform of glacial ice on the western side of the Antarctic Peninsula, has been destabilizing for years. Satellite images show that the shelf’s last major stabilizing connection — an ice bridge linking **Charcot Island** and **Latady Island** — has fractured and broken apart, leaving the shelf increasingly exposed to waves, currents and further disintegration.

Before recent losses, the Wilkins Ice Shelf covered roughly **13,000 to 16,000 square kilometers** — an area often compared to **Connecticut** or **Northern Ireland**. While much of the shelf remains in place, scientists warn that the collapse of key support points could trigger a much larger breakup.

“This is the kind of event we have been watching for,” one polar researcher said. “Once an ice shelf loses the pinning points and ice bridges that hold it together, it can fracture very quickly.”

## A Shelf Held Together by Islands

The Wilkins Ice Shelf occupies a region of the southwest Antarctic Peninsula, bordered and stabilized by nearby landmasses including **Charcot Island**, **Latady Island** and **Alexander Island**. For years, a narrow strip of floating ice between Charcot and Latady acted like a brace, helping prevent the shelf from opening fully to ocean swell.

That bridge had been thinning and cracking steadily. As it narrowed, satellite imagery revealed long fractures spreading across the shelf surface. Its breakup has raised fears that large sections of the shelf could now detach in the coming days, weeks or months.

## Major Losses in 2008

The warning signs became unmistakable in **2008**, when the Wilkins Ice Shelf suffered a series of large breakups. In that year alone, it lost an estimated **1,800 square kilometers** of ice — hundreds of square miles — during multiple collapse events.

In early 2008, a section hundreds of square kilometers in size disintegrated rapidly, splintering into a field of icebergs and smaller fragments. Additional losses followed later in the year, leaving the remaining ice bridge thinner and weaker. By the end of 2008, scientists said the shelf had entered a far more vulnerable state.

Those events were part of a broader pattern of ice-shelf retreat around the Antarctic Peninsula, one of the fastest-warming regions on Earth over the late 20th century.

## What Ice Shelves Are — and Why They Matter

Ice shelves are thick, floating extensions of glaciers and ice sheets. They form where land-based ice flows outward from the continent and spreads over the ocean. Because they are already floating, their collapse does **not directly raise sea levels** in the same way that melting land ice does.

But ice shelves play a critical role as natural brakes. They can **buttress** glaciers behind them, slowing the flow of land ice into the sea. When an ice shelf breaks apart, glaciers feeding it may accelerate, sending more land-based ice into the ocean and contributing to sea-level rise over time.

Scientists have seen this pattern before. The collapse of other Antarctic Peninsula ice shelves, including parts of the Larsen system, was followed by acceleration of glaciers that had once been restrained by the floating ice.

## Climate and Ocean Forces Under Scrutiny

Researchers say the Wilkins breakup cannot be attributed to a single cause, but several factors are believed to be involved: atmospheric warming, surface meltwater, ocean-driven thinning and mechanical stress from waves and tides.

Surface melting can be especially damaging. When meltwater collects in crevasses, it can force cracks deeper through the ice in a process called **hydrofracturing**. Warmer ocean water can also thin ice shelves from below, weakening them long before they visibly break apart.

The Antarctic Peninsula has experienced pronounced warming in recent decades, and many ice shelves along its coast have retreated or collapsed. While conditions vary across Antarctica, the Wilkins event is being viewed as another sign of how sensitive floating ice shelves can be to changing climate and ocean conditions.

## Scientists Watching Closely

Polar scientists are continuing to monitor the Wilkins Ice Shelf using satellite radar and optical imagery, which allow them to track cracks, rifts and calving events even in remote regions and during poor weather.

The immediate question is whether the breakup of the Charcot-Latady ice bridge will trigger a wider collapse or whether remaining portions of the shelf will stabilize temporarily.

Either way, researchers say the Wilkins Ice Shelf has crossed an important threshold.

“This is not just a single iceberg calving,” a scientist familiar with the observations said. “It is the weakening of an entire ice-shelf system.”

For now, the shelf remains under intense observation as fractures widen and the Antarctic summer melt season continues to test one of the continent’s most fragile floating ice platforms.

Antarctica’s Wilkins Ice Shelf, a large floating platform of ice on the western side of the Antarctic Peninsula, has begun retreating after remaining relatively stable for decades, scientists report. Satellite observations show new fractures, ice loss, and weakening along parts of the shelf, raising concerns that the region is continuing to respond to long-term warming trends.

Researchers say the retreat may be linked to rising air and ocean temperatures around the Antarctic Peninsula, one of the fastest-warming areas in the Southern Hemisphere during the late 20th century. Warmer conditions can melt the surface of an ice shelf, allowing water to drain into cracks and force them open. Warmer ocean water can also thin the shelf from below, reducing its strength and making it more vulnerable to breakup.

The environmental impacts could be significant for the local Antarctic ecosystem. Ice shelves help shape coastal habitats by influencing sea-ice formation, ocean circulation, and the distribution of nutrients. Their retreat can change conditions for plankton, krill, fish, penguins, seals, and other wildlife that depend on stable sea-ice and marine food webs.

However, the retreat of the Wilkins Ice Shelf will not directly raise global sea levels. That is because the shelf is already floating in the ocean, much like ice cubes in a glass of water. When floating ice melts, it does not add new water to the ocean. Scientists are more concerned about ice shelves because they can act as barriers that slow land-based glaciers. If an ice shelf collapses and allows glaciers behind it to flow faster into the sea, that land ice could contribute to future sea-level rise.

For now, the Wilkins retreat is seen as another sign of rapid environmental change along the Antarctic Peninsula and a reminder that ice shelves can weaken suddenly after long periods of apparent stability.
